description: We are computer science students at Haigazian University.
summary:
Perilune is a first-person educational space mission game built in Unity 6. The player carries a survey instrument to a station in lunar orbit and must scan a patch of the Moon before it passes out of view.

A run starts at the main menu, then a tutorial that teaches the controls and stages a practice emergency. The player picks one of five missions, from very easy to very hard, each with its own target, risk level and recommended supplies. Three scenes follow: suiting up, packing five supplies and launching; flying the docking approach to the station; and running the survey itself.

During the survey, faults strike at random: power loss, overheating, corrupted computer memory, a dropped radio link. Each is a short keyboard minigame rated Clean, Partial or Botched. Harder missions and missing supplies make faults more likely. After any mishap the game explains why it happens in real spaceflight and what to do next time.

A mission report then grades coverage, data quality and downlink against the mission’s goals and shows which choices made the difference.
details:
What it does

Perilune is a first-person educational game about flying a complete space mission. The player delivers a survey instrument to a station in orbit around the Moon and must scan a target on the surface before it passes out of view.

A run begins with a tutorial that teaches the controls and stages a practice emergency. The player then chooses one of five missions, from very easy to very hard, each with its own target, time limit, risk level and recommended supplies. Three playable scenes follow: suiting up, packing five supplies and launching; flying the docking approach to the station; and running the survey. During the survey, faults strike at random: the cooling pump loses power, the detector overheats, radiation corrupts the computer’s memory, the radio link to Earth drops. Each fault is a short hands-on task rated Clean, Partial or Botched. A mission report then grades the result against the mission’s goals and shows which decisions made the difference.

Benefits and intended impact

The game teaches that spaceflight is about preparation and trade-offs with limited resources. Only five supplies fit in the pack, so the player must decide what to bring before knowing what will go wrong. Whenever something goes wrong, the game explains why that problem is real in space and what to do differently next time. Our aim is for students to finish a run understanding why spacecraft need radiators, error-checking memory, power budgets and careful docking, because they have dealt with each one themselves.

Tools

Unity 6 with the Universal Render Pipeline, C#, UI Toolkit for all menus and task screens, and Unity’s Input System. Sound effects are synthesized from scratch by a Python script. We used Claude Code as a coding assistant.

Creativity

Every fault is modelled on a real spacecraft system and turned into its own small puzzle, such as checking parity bits to find corrupted memory or shedding electrical loads to fit a backup power feed. Faults are rolled from the mission’s difficulty and the supplies packed, so no two runs are the same and early choices have visible consequences later.

What we considered

We grounded the design in NASA material on mission planning and CubeSat development. After playtesting showed our first mission briefing was too complicated, we replaced it with a simple choice of missions. We kept all instructions in plain language and added a tutorial so a first-time player is never left guessing.
